title: Butler stares down backlash over health insurance rebate
full_text:
Health Minister Mark Butler is staring down a growing backlash against his plans to cut the more generous private health insurance rebate for over-65s, as the states say their public hospitals won’t be able to deal with a “sudden shift” in patients dropping private healthcare.
With the Albanese government keen to get its private health insurance reforms through parliament in the final sitting fortnight of the year, the states on Wednesday demanded assurances the overhaul wouldn’t put a greater burden on public hospitals if private patients decided to cancel or downgrade their cover because of the changes.
The furore over the government’s scrapping over the higher private health insurance rebate for older Australians comes as the Senate could delay a vote on Labor’s capital gains tax changes for business and start-ups until next year, with the Greens considering supporting an inquiry and examining a proposal by Community Strong Australia MP Allegra Spender.
State ministers said they had regularly raised concerns with Mr Butler about federal Labor’s decision to scrap the Howard-era private health insurance rebate for older people and redirect $3bn in savings into aged care.
New Ipsos polling released on Wednesday and first reported in The Australian, showing the number of older Australians who would cancel their private health insurance because of the changes was eight times what Labor initially anticipated, reignited a nationwide political pushback.
South Australian Labor Health Minister Blair Boyer said he had told the commonwealth its changes could place significant pressures on the state’s public hospital system, with modelling provided by SA Health indicating extra annual costs up to $60.2m.
“More than 226,000 South Australians aged 65 and over hold private health insurance and they are among the highest users of hospital services,” Mr Boyer said.
“We need assurance that our public hospitals will not be left carrying additional demand if older South Australians decide private health cover is no longer affordable. South Australia has the oldest population per capita on the mainland, and we cannot afford changes that shift additional pressure on to a public hospital system that is already managing significant demand.”
NSW Labor Health Minister Ryan Park said it wasn’t fair on Australians who had paid for their private healthcare for a long time to be forced to pay more, blaming the Albanese government in part for “significant challenges” facing public hospitals.
“It is a concern of mine when we have big increases in demand already, when we’re dealing with a lot of older patients who shouldn’t be in our hospitals, (who are) stuck in our hospitals, for there to be another policy lever that encourages more people to use a public system when they were being delivered health services for many years through a private system they had made a decision to pay for,” Mr Park told ABC radio.
“I can’t see a sudden shift of people going into the public system where they’ve been paying private healthcare for some of these people 40 or 50 years of their life.”
Tasmanian Liberal Health Minister Bridget Archer urged federal Labor to scrap its “toxic policy”, cautioning it would increase pressure on state hospitals and waiting times. “Older Tasmanians shouldn’t be slugged with higher fees to pay for the federal government’s ongoing lack of action on aged care,” she said.
“Even worse, it will just put more pressure on public hospital EDs, ambulances, and elective surgery waiting times by forcing older Tasmanians to drop their cover.”
Queensland Liberal National Party Health Minister Tim Nicholls said he’d been “loud and clear” with the commonwealth about the pressure he expected the “ill thought through” policy would have on already busy public hospitals. “This additional pressure will add to the thousands of older Australians already stuck in hospitals right across the country because the commonwealth is failing in its duty of care to provide adequate aged-care supports,” he said.
Mr Butler hit back, saying state ministers should “pay more attention to commonwealth government and independent modelling than to self-serving modelling presented by the private health insurance industry”.
The Ipsos polling was commissioned by Members Health Fund Alliance, the national peak body for not-for-profit and member-owned health funds.
“Government modelling and independent modelling from the University of Melbourne suggest this measure will have a very small impact on health membership, which will continue to grow over coming years,” Mr Butler said. “The industry has a record of presenting modelling that suggests dramatic impacts from changes to insurance rebate arrangements that never eventuate.”
Noting Mr Butler had conceded he’d made a hard choice to take money from Australians’ private health insurance rebates and put it into aged care, opposition health spokeswoman Anne Ruston said he was forcing older people into much harder choices about their healthcare.
With the Coalition staunchly opposed to the bill, which has already been discharged from the Senate notice paper once, Mr Butler must exempt all pensioners in order to get the Greens on side.
Greens leader David Shoebridge wouldn’t say whether the government was willing to accept their demand as negotiations continued. “We have said to the government: you carve out all pensioners, and you can get some significant budget savings here. It’s up to them whether they want to accept that offer,” Senator Shoebridge said.
Greens Treasury spokesman Nick McKim said it was still a possibility the Senate could vote to send the government’s CGT changes to an inquiry over the summer to scrutinise Ms Spender’s alternative plan, which reduces the CGT discount to 40 per cent for “productive assets”.
The government’s legislative priorities for the final sitting fortnight include the private health insurance changes, the digital duty of care regime, the domestic gas reservation and a minimum tax on discretionary trusts.
Additional reporting: Matthew Denholm Lydia Lynch
